notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa033c.opp-l: Line 2: the scan's 'interprecctur' is read as 'interprecetur' (intercede in prayer); 'interpretetur' (interpret on my behalf) is also conceivable. Line 3: the sentence on Melchizedek is awkward as printed; 'justitia' is taken as 'justitiam' or an equivalent, with Scripture as the understood subject. Line 4: the verse number of the Daniel reference is lost in the scan (the passage is Dan. 9:24). 'Quod si non Mariae congruit' at the end of chapter III is translated as printed; the sense suggests the author may mean 'even if not to Mary', and the text may be disturbed. The printed reference 'Luc. I, 55' is read as Luke 1:35, and 'pulvis est' at Gen. 3:19 as 'pulvis es'.

Line 1: the printed "nolo ut sint unum" is read as "volo", as the sense requires; the verse is John 17:11. The closing passage "ha- borei e vult, ae per hec Iotust" is badly garbled and is read as "habere vult, ac per hoc potest" ("wills to have ... and therefore can"); the reconstruction is probable but not certain. "Non quantum pertinet ad aequam administrationem" is obscure; "equal administration" is literal, perhaps meaning equality of office or authority between mother and son. Line 2: "thalamum cali Domini" is read as "caeli Domini" ("the Lord of heaven"). The sentence "Illud ergo sacratissimum corpus ... pulveris" is loosely constructed; "communi sorte" may mean either that the common lot is what terrifies the author or that the body was handed over by that common lot. "Quod" after "de proprio" is taken as referring to the author's own body. Line 3: "munstram Chi isti" is read as "ministram Christi". In "ut concepto et nato", "ut" is taken as "as [when]". "Numquid aequali gratia" is rendered as an expected yes, as the next clause requires, though "numquid" usually expects no.

Line 9: 'Haec cuncta quae diximus, quia naturam servantia non cognoscimus' is awkward, and a footnote mark stands after 'naturam'; the sense seems to be that these miracles did not follow nature, but the reading is uncertain. 'omnia sunt quae sunt velle' seems corrupt, and the rendering is tentative; the point seems to be that Christ's power extends to all that he wills, and that he wills what is just and worthy. 'tantum tantum filium' seems to be a doubled word or a corruption (perhaps 'tantum talem'), and is rendered 'so great a son'. Line 10: 'prolernt' is read as 'proferat'; a footnote mark follows 'praesumpsi'.

nodes.text: ONE BOOK ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.
BY AN UNCERTAIN BUT DEVOUT AUTHOR.

PREFACE. A prayer for divine light in order to speak worthily. Being about to answer what I understand concerning the questions put to me about the temporal dissolution and the everlasting assumption of the Virgin and Mother of the Lord, I implore you with suppliant prayer, God, almighty Father: you who command the clouds and they rain showers, who touch the mountains and they smoke, who open the earth and it sprouts, command what I am to say, grant what I am to bring forth, and reveal where I am to direct my discourse. For it is a venerable thing to me, Lord, and most worthy of reverence in my inmost heart, to speak of the mother of your Son, and to employ my tongue in discourse on her most holy body, she who alone was found worthy to receive God and man, in order to give him birth, having been made the throne of God and the hall of the eternal king, according to what you have taught us through your holy Patriarchs, Prophets and Apostles, by figures and by words: we have believed them, and are certain; for you have never deceived, you who know neither how to be deceived nor how to deceive, showing that your Son, coeternal and consubstantial with you, was to be incarnate, and was incarnate through the Virgin's womb, from which he who created all bodily things with you took flesh, the author [taking it] from a handmaid, and God made man from a human being; taking from her his nature, not his origin, while your Holy Spirit sanctified a human womb in her, and purified and cleansed it for the conception of your Son. The effect of this dignity and grace neither the heart can conceive nor the tongue express. For no conception and no birth but such as this had befitted God, who had come to redeem those whom he willed to create; to create above all by majesty, to redeem by humility: taking from a sanctified body a holy nature of humility, and an immaculate one from an immaculate [body]. For the ineffable grace of sanctification which he granted when he was to be conceived, he did not take away when conceived and born. How much it availed in the Virgin's body is best known to him alone who from her nature took up the nature he had made. Through him I beg you, Lord, since through him you bestow all good things, which you choose to bestow, to grant that I may speak of such great holiness without offence. Even if not the whole may be said as it is, which is impossible for every human tongue, yet let what it is in part be said as it is. Let the most precious, then, sound forth with true preciousness, the most holy with sure holiness, the most inestimable with most faithful truth. And since these things exceed human reason, may your Spirit be present, to lead us by his sacred breath into all truth of what is to be said: so that, since we must speak of that body and soul which he sanctified beyond natural use, and on which he conferred grace, he may not allow us to say what is foreign to them, but what is proper to them: to the praise and glory of you, God, almighty Father, and to the honour of your Son, born of the Virgin, and of the same Holy Spirit, our God and Lord, with whom yours is the kingdom and the rule for all ages of ages. Amen.

CHAPTER ONE. The author is a lover of truth. In the Scriptures some things are to be expounded in one way, others in another. Since I am about to answer a question most profound and most exalted in its dignity, I beseech my reader to intercede for me, and, if he recognizes anything said fully by me, to be grateful for the gifts of God; but if less so, to have compassion on our lowliness; for although we are less able, yet we undoubtedly desire what is true. Undertaking, then, to speak, as far as the Lord may grant, of the assumption of the most holy body of Mary, perpetual virgin, and of her sacred soul, we say this first: that in the divine Scriptures, after the Lord on the cross entrusted his mother to the disciple (John 19:27), so that chastity might be safeguarded by chaste services, nothing is found about her except what Luke records in the Acts of the Apostles, after naming these same [apostles] by name, saying: All these were persevering with one accord in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers (Acts 1:14). We say this because great matters must be handled the more cautiously, the less they can be clearly confirmed by specific testimonies of authorities. But since holy Scripture has left certain things to be sought by the labours of inquiry, they are not to be considered superfluous, so long as they have been brought to light by true inquiry. For the authority of truth is fruitful: and when it is diligently examined, it is known to beget from itself what it itself is. For often, when examined, it brings forth a true fittingness which it hides in plain words; and often it conveys things in open words, in which it invites us to seek nothing beyond what it has sounded: as in this, that Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, Jacob begot Judah and his brothers (Matt. 1:2), and other such things, in which the letter alone is to be held. But some things it commends in such a way as to convey both the letter and a mystical understanding together: as in the crossing of the Red Sea, and the heavenly manna, and the tabernacle of God, and the ark of the covenant, where a figure of things to come was shown, namely the special privilege of the Baptism of Christ and of the Church. Some things [it commends] only mystically, as when it says that God breathed into the face of Adam the breath of life, though he has no mouth for breathing, nor hands for working, although the prophet says, Your hands, Lord, have made me and fashioned me (Job 10:8)

CHAPTER II. There are truths about which Scripture is silent, but not reason. Among them is the assumption of the Blessed Mary. There are also certain things which, although they have been wholly omitted from record, are nevertheless believed by true reason, to which the very fittingness of the matter is believed [to lead], as a guide and forerunner. For it says nothing of the righteousness of Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, although those very merits deserving such great praise are recognized to have come first. It commends nothing about the happiness of the life of Enoch and Elijah after they were carried off, though all know clearly that those whom the Lord willed to carry off from here, to be kept for the future, live in blessedness. What then is to be said of Mary's death, what of her assumption, on which divine Scripture commends nothing, unless we must seek by reason what accords with truth; and let truth itself become authority, without which authority necessarily has no force either? For, mindful of the human condition, we are not afraid to say that she underwent that temporal death which her Son himself, who is both God and man, certainly bore by the law of the human lot: and this because the man was taken up from her womb and poured forth from it.

CHAPTER III. Whether it is fitting that the body of the Blessed Mary was dissolved into dust. This does not follow from the curse on Adam. But if we say that she is held by the bonds of death, and dissolved into the common putrefaction, worm and ash, it must be weighed whether this befits such great holiness, the prerogative of so great a hall of God. For we know that it was said to the first parent: Because you are dust and to dust you shall go (Gen. 3:19). If this is said of death, the sentence is general; if of dissolution into dust, this condition was escaped by the flesh of Christ, taken from the flesh of Mary, which did not undergo corruption. For about this it is written through the prophet David, who says: For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption (Ps. 15:10). And of what holy one this was said the archangel made known, who said to Mary: And the holy one that will be born of you will be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). Truly holy, and the holy of holies: whence also that [place] is called the Holy of Holies which kept those things by which he was prefigured, who alone is truly called the Holy of Holies. For this is he of whom the same archangel Gabriel speaks to Daniel, saying, among the other things to come that he showed: And let the vision and prophecy be fulfilled, and let the Holy of Holies be anointed (Dan. 9). For this Holy One did not see corruption, who on the third day, returning in triumph from the underworld, rose again. His flesh, which was taken from Mary, though it died from weakness, came to life again from the power of God. But this [was the doing of] him who had power to die when he willed and to rise when he willed. Therefore the nature taken from the Virgin is excepted from that general sentence. And if this does not suit Mary, yet it suits the Son whom she bore.

CHAPTER IV. Mary is free from the curse on Eve. After these things said to Adam, from which the Son of Mary is excepted, we must consider the things said also to Eve, whether they are general to all women, and whether Mary is excepted in any respect. For it is written: To the woman also God said: I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions. In pain you will bear children, and you will be under the power of a man, and he will rule over you (Gen. 3:16). Mary endured hardship, she whose soul the sword of Christ's passion pierced (Luke 2:35): but she did not multiply conceptions, nor did she live under the power of a man, that is, of a husband, she who with wholly intact womb received Christ from the Holy Spirit, and, the integrity of her virginity remaining, continued a virgin. Since she received him without the filth of sin, and without the loss that comes of union with a man, she bore him without pain, and without violation of her integrity she remained whole in the modesty of her virginity. For he could accomplish this in the case of his mother, because God so chose to be born of a human being. So although Mary shares in the hardships of Eve, she does not share in giving birth with pain. For her singular holiness merited this, and the singular grace by which she was singularly judged worthy to receive God. Not undeservedly, then, is she excepted by true judgement from certain general [sentences], she whom such great grace preserves and the prerogative of her dignity exalts. For how much the power of Christ can do, the whole of the world shows; how much his grace can do, the integrity of Mary shows: which, just as it differs from nature, so differs from common use. What then, if amid so great a difference we say that she, through whom God willed to be born and to share the substance of flesh, underwent the death of the human lot and yet was not held by its bonds: will that be impious? For we know that Jesus can do all things, who says of himself: All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18).

CHAPTER V. Christ is to be believed to have honoured his mother in this. Indeed, his own nature. The unity of grace with Christ. Mary's special unity with Christ. If, then, he willed to keep his mother intact in the modesty of her virginity, why would he not will to keep her uncorrupted by the stench of decay? Let him who has known the mind of the Lord, and who has been his counsellor, say: does it not belong to the kindness of the Lord to preserve the honour of his mother, he who had come not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matt. 5:17)? For the law, just as it commands honour for a mother, so condemns dishonour. For it is pious to believe that he who in life honoured her before all others with the grace of conceiving him honoured her in death with a singular salvation and a special grace. For he who, being born from her, was able to leave her a virgin was able to make her a stranger to decay and dust. For decay and the worm are the disgrace of the human condition, and since Jesus is a stranger to this disgrace, the nature of Mary is excepted, which Jesus is shown to have taken from her. For the flesh of Jesus is the flesh of Mary, and much more specially than Joseph was the flesh of Judah and his other brothers, to whom he said: For he is our brother and our flesh (Gen. 37:27). For the flesh of Christ, although it was magnified by the glory of the resurrection and glorified by a mighty ascension above all the heavens, nevertheless remained and remains the same nature of flesh that was taken from Mary. For he himself it is who was conceived and born, and raised from the dead through the glory of the Father: just as he himself indeed testifies after the resurrection, when he says to the apostles: See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself (Luke 24:39). For what does "it is I myself" mean, unless that I am no other than the one who I was then, when I suffered? This you can indeed recognize, you who recognize the wounds of the nails in my hands and feet. He, therefore, the very same, ascended the heavens, and carried the flesh that he took from his mother beyond the stars, honouring all human nature, and much more his mother's. If, then, the son is the nature of the mother, it is fitting that the mother also be [the nature] of the son, not as regards equal administration, but as regards the same reciprocal substance: as man from man, flesh from flesh, mother from son, son from mother, not to unity of person, but to unity of bodily nature and substance. For if grace can bring about unity without the property of a special nature, how much more where there is unity of grace and also the special birth of the body? For there is a unity of grace, such as that of the disciples in Christ, of whom he himself said: Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me; I will that they be one, as we also are. And again, of all the righteous: I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you: that is, that they may be through grace what we are through the nature of divinity. Indeed, if this unity of grace, which is kept for all who believe in Christ, is not taken away from Mary even in the judgement of the less wise, how much more when, together with the unity of grace, the very specialness of nature makes mother and son, son and mother, one? We must also see what he went on to add concerning those whom he willed to be one with himself through grace. For he says: Holy Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my radiance which you have given me (John 17:11, 20, etc.). O great and inestimable goodness of God, who wills to have his own with him in glory, that they may enjoy his radiance, they who, joined here by their faith, are judged worthy to be one with him! If, then, he wills to have them with him, and therefore can, he who can do all things, what is to be thought of his mother, where she is worthy to be kept, if not in the presence of her Son?

CHAPTER VI. Mary's body already in heaven in two ways. As far, then, as I perceive, as far as I understand, as far as I believe, Mary's soul enjoys the radiance of Christ and the glorious sight of him; ever thirsting to see and ever beholding, while she is inestimably fed, she is honoured by her Son with a certain more excellent and special prerogative: possessing in Christ her own body which she bore, glorified at the right hand of the Father; and if not her own [body] through which she bore [him], yet her own [body] which she bore. And why not her own [body] through which she bore [him]? Unless some authority not yet examined stands in the way, I truly believe [that she possesses] also that through which she bore [him]; for such great sanctification is more worthy of heaven than of earth. It is fitting that the throne of God, the bridal chamber of the Lord of heaven, the house and tabernacle of Christ, should be where he himself is. For it is more fitting that heaven should keep so precious a treasure than earth; such great integrity is rightly followed by incorruptibility, not by any dissolution in decay. As for that most sacred body, then, from which Christ took flesh, and united the divine nature to the human, not losing what he was but taking on what he was not, so that the Word might become flesh, that is, God might become man, because I cannot conceive that it was handed over as food for worms, I am terrified to say [so], by the common lot of decay and of the dust to come from worms. If I thought nothing higher of it than of my own [body], I would say nothing other than [I say] of my own. For this, without any doubt, is to be dissolved in death, and after death is to become decay, after decay the worm, after the worm, as is fitting, the most abject dust. This does not seem something that can be accepted as believable of Mary, because the gift of incomparable grace drives that judgement far away.

CHAPTER VII. It is inferred from Christ's petition for his servants. Angels served Christ on earth. The consideration of many things invites me to say this, among which is what Truth himself once said to his servants: Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also (John 12:26). For if this is the general pronouncement concerning all who serve Christ through faith and pious work, how much more, and in how special a manner, concerning Mary? For everyone of sound mind understands that Mary was the servant of Christ, by the showing of her work and by the most unbending truth of her faith. For beyond doubt she who carried him in her womb, and nourished and cherished him when he was brought forth at birth, and, as the Gospel says, laid him in a manger (Luke 2:7), and, fleeing from the face of Herod, hid him in Egypt (Matt. 2:13), and attended all his infancy with a mother's affection, proved a servant in deed; so much so that even as far as the cross, on which she saw her son, now a grown man, hanging, she undoubtedly did not withdraw from following him, not only with the steps of her feet, as if out of reverence for the Lord, but also with the affection of imitation. Mary, then, just as she proved a most devoted servant of Christ in the qualities of special works, so beyond doubt she was his follower in the faith of religion and the charity of true belief. For she could not but believe in his divinity, she who knew that she had conceived him not by male seed according to the order of nature, but by the divine breath, as the Archangel announced: seeing always the crowd of angels attending him in service, as when he was conceived and born, namely when there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, crying and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will (Luke 2:14); and when he was about to flee into Egypt and to return from there again: from which she could clearly know that such services were fitting for none but God. Hence also the announcement of the star, and the unexpected bringing of the Magi from the farthest regions, were for her the greatest evidence of the truth. Likewise also the meeting with Simeon and Anna, in their prophetic dignity, unaccustomed for others and special for him. All these things Mary indeed kept, and, strengthened by them all more deeply in faith, pondered them in her pious heart: so much so that, not wavering at all, but certain of her son's power as of the true power of God, she said when the wine ran out at the wedding: They have no wine (John 2:3), plainly knowing that he could do this, which it soon came about that he accomplished by a divine miracle. See, then, Mary, the servant of Christ in faith and in work, and his devoted follower up to his death, not more in step than, as we must believe, in the affection of imitation: if she will not be there where Christ wills his servants to be, where then will she be? And if there, will it surely be with equal grace? And if with equal grace, where is the just judgement of God, who renders to each according to his merits? If, then, grace was deservedly given to Mary living before all others, will it be diminished for her dead? Far from it: for if the death of all the saints is precious, Mary's is surely most precious, whom such great grace accompanied that she is called, and is, the mother of God.

CHAPTER VIII. Christ was able to keep Mary without corruption. He willed it, because it was fitting. All these things having been considered, then, and with true reason, I judge that we must confess that Mary is in Christ and with Christ: in Christ, because in him we live, move and are; with Christ, gloriously assumed to the joys of eternity, received by the kindness of Christ with greater honour than the rest, as grace here honoured her above the rest; and that she who bore her own and everyone's Saviour was not brought after death to the common lowliness, that is, of decay and worm and dust. If it is in his power that not a hair of the saints' heads should perish, it is also in his power to keep her whole in soul and body. If none of the Church's people doubts his power, that he can keep his mother without corruption for ever, why should it be doubted that he willed it, so far as concerns the grace of such great kindness? If the divine will chose, by grace alone, among the crackling flames of raging fires, to keep not only the bodies of the boys unharmed but even their very garments unburnt, why should it refuse in the case of his own mother what it chose in the case of another's garment? Mercy alone willed to keep Jonah uncorrupted in the belly of the whale, contrary to natural course (Jon. 2:1). Will grace not keep Mary uncorrupted, beyond nature? Daniel was kept from the unrestrained hunger of the lions (Dan. 6:22); is Mary, endowed with such great merits of dignity, not to be kept? All these things we have spoken of, because we do not recognise them as observing nature: we do not doubt that in Mary's integrity grace could do more than nature. For the things we speak of are works of divinity, and they are therefore possible, because they come from omnipotence. And Christ is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, to whom belong all things that are the Father's; all things are his that are to will; and to will all things that are just and worthy. And for this reason it seems that Mary worthily rejoices with unspeakable joy in soul and body, in her own son, with her own son, through her own son, and that no hardship of corruption ought to follow her, whom no corruption of her integrity followed in bearing so great a son: so that she who was flooded with such great grace may be for ever uncorrupted; that she who bore the whole and perfect life of all may live whole; that she may be with him whom she carried in her womb; that she may be beside him, she who bore, cherished and nourished him, Mary, the mother of God, the nurse of God, the servant of God and the follower of God: concerning whom, as I have already said, because I do not dare to think otherwise, I do not presume to speak otherwise.

CHAPTER IX. In what spirit the author has asserted the foregoing. Let your brotherly Charity therefore receive this view, according as the Spirit of Christ has inspired [it]. The things that urged me to speak in this way have been shown in part. But if anyone chooses to oppose them, since he will not want to say that Christ cannot do these things, let him set forth why it is not fitting that he should will them, and for this reason that they are not so. And if he shows that he truly knows the counsel of God on these matters, I will begin to believe him concerning things about which I have not presumed to think otherwise; and I will marvel that he has searched out the depth of the divine counsel, which it seems to me that I ought, with due reverence, to marvel at with the Apostle, who says: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are his judgements, and his ways unsearchable (Rom. 11:33)! And because, according to the same Apostle, we know in part and we prophesy in part (1 Cor. 13:9), I have spoken about these matters, if not as much as there is [to say], yet in the way I believed I ought to speak. If, then, what I have written is true, I give thanks to you, Christ, because I could not think of the holy Virgin, your mother, anything but what seemed pious and worthy. If, then, I have spoken as I ought, approve it, Christ, I beseech you, you and yours; but if as I ought not, forgive it, you and yours! You who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.
